title: Is Atherosclerosis Induced by Defective Methylation Pathways? A Role for Lipid Peroxidation in Protecting Mitochondria from Deuterium Overload
content: Atherosclerosis, the leading cause of death, is the slow accumulation of oxidized lipids in the artery walls, eventually leading to heart attacks and stroke. Despite much study, the underlying pathology remains poorly understood. We hypothesize that atherosclerosis develops due to deuterium overload in mitochondria, systemically, and that the accumulation of lipids in the atheroma ameliorates this problem. We show the critical role that gut microbes play in supplying deuterium-depleted nutrients to the mitochondria, in large part through the supply of methyl groups and short chain fatty acids. Deuterium (2H), a natural heavy isotope of protium,  damages the ATP synthase nanomotors that produce ATP. Gut microbes exploit hydrogen gas recycling to deplete deuterium in derived metabolites. Gut dysbiosis impairs this process. The bis-allylic carbon atoms in polyunsaturated fatty acids (PUFAs) have a unique property that allows them to trap and sequester deuterium. A defective methylation system, reflected in high plasma trimethylamine oxide (TMAO), leads, through complex signaling processes, to the trapping of lipids in the artery wall and the induction of an inflammatory response to promote lipid peroxidation chain reactions.  Deficiencies in aldehyde dehydrogenases lead to increased exposure to formaldehyde, acetaldehyde, and malondialdehyde, causing tissue damage. Over time, deuterium loading at the bis-allylic carbon atoms quenches the cascade, stabilizing the plaque. This theory can explain most of the markers associated with cardiovascular disease (CVD), including TMAO, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), homocysteine, malondialdehyde, psychological and emotional stress, dimethylglycine, and deficiencies in glutathione, zinc and B vitamins.
